questions.q: What specific problem does the 'one trigger per object' pattern solve?
options: It makes Apex code run faster in every case
Multiple triggers on the same object have execution order that the architect doesn't directly control, which makes behavior unpredictable as more triggers get added over time
It removes the need for any Apex test classes
It allows an object to bypass governor limits entirely
questions.explain: With a single trigger per object delegating to a handler class, the architect controls execution order directly, instead of depending on an unpredictable, uncontrolled order across multiple separate triggers.

questions.q: In the domain/selector/service layering pattern described in this lesson, what is the selector layer responsible for?
options: Orchestrating a business process across multiple objects
Building and executing SOQL queries for one object, so query logic isn't duplicated across the codebase
Rendering Lightning web components on the page
Defining page layouts and record types
questions.explain: The selector layer owns SOQL queries for one object in one place, so bulkification and query logic are handled centrally rather than duplicated across many classes.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a service layer exist separately from a domain layer?
options: Because a business process that touches multiple objects together doesn't fully belong inside any single object's domain class -- it belongs in a service method that coordinates across objects
Because service layers are purely a naming convention with no functional difference from domain layers
Because the service layer replaces the need for a selector layer entirely
Because domain layers are deprecated in current Salesforce architecture guidance
questions.explain: The domain layer owns logic specific to one object's own records; the service layer owns orchestration of a process that spans multiple objects, which doesn't cleanly belong inside any single object's domain class.

questions.q: What is a 'subflow,' as described in this lesson, and what problem does it solve?
options: A Flow that runs only in sandbox orgs, never in production
A reusable Flow called from within another Flow -- the declarative analogue of a shared method, avoiding duplicating the same logic across multiple automations
A subflow is another name for a validation rule
A type of Apex trigger that runs before the main trigger
questions.explain: A subflow lets shared logic (like a standard notification process) be built once and referenced from multiple Flows, instead of being duplicated with the inevitable drift that follows duplicated logic.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue an Application Architect needs to understand these patterns, not just leave them entirely to developers?
options: Because architects are required to write 100% of the Apex code themselves
Because understanding why a pattern exists lets the architect credibly review a design, catch a violation early, and explain the real cost of shortcuts like adding one more trigger
Because these patterns have no actual effect on code quality, so understanding them is optional
Because only developers are allowed to use Custom Metadata Types
questions.explain: The lesson frames pattern knowledge as a review and judgment tool for the architect -- being able to catch and explain why a shortcut like an extra trigger has a real, specific cost, not a requirement to personally write all the code.
